title: No Running Lights
passages:
Rain came at the Marrow sideways, and nobody had the deck lights on, because Sol had killed them at dusk to save the batteries and because a boat that shows itself on the drowned coast gets visited. So the deck was lit only by the wheelhouse instruments and the green wash of Wren's slate, which she held in both hands against her chest like a cat she was keeping warm.

The slate did two jobs. Its recorder logged every diver's suit telemetry—depth and air and heart rate—so Wren could sit afterward and rebuild the hours a person lost down there, frame by frame, out of the data their body had kept even when their head hadn't. Its other job was the radar sweep, a thin green line crawling around the screen once every four seconds, pinging anything solid within half a mile and painting it a smudge.

The smudge showed up on the blind side, port quarter, three hundred meters and closing.

"Rusk," Dey said, from where he sat on an upturned crate with his rig open in his lap. He wasn't working on it. There was nothing left to work on; his scrubber cartridge—the canister that pulls carbon dioxide back out of a diver's rebreathed air—was in Teo's chest, and without it Dey could not go below ten meters without poisoning himself. He kept the rig open anyway, the way a man holds his hat in his hands at a burial.

"You can't see anything," Wren said.

"I can't see anything," Dey agreed. "So it's Rusk."

Sol came out of the wheelhouse with a mug she wasn't drinking from. "How close?"

"Two-eighty. Two-sixty." Wren tilted the slate. "He's not lit. No lamp, no masthead, nothing."

"Course?"

"Coming around our stern. Slow. Like a man who's already decided where he's going to stand."

Nia stood in the wheelhouse doorway with her brother behind her, one hand back on Teo's shoulder to keep him in the room. Teo was eleven and had the loose, too-quiet stillness of a kid whose medicine was down to the last few cartridges, and Nia watched the dark the way she watched everything, like it owed her money. "Then he can stay off my boat," she said.

"It's not your boat," Dey said.

"It's not his either."

Wren swept again. Two-ten. She could hear it under the rain now, the low lump of a barge engine running slow, no rhythm to it, no horn. Barge skippers on the coast ran lights because the alternative was another hull through their wheelhouse. This one had the lights off on purpose. That took a kind of confidence Wren didn't like, and it cost nothing, which she liked less.

"He'll hail before we see him," she said.

"Who always hails?"

"Nobody. People who come to take things."

Sol drank nothing from her mug. "Get below, both kids."

"I'm not going below," Nia said.

"Then stand behind me and be quiet, which is a thing you have never once done."

Wren watched the sweep. One-sixty. One-forty. Rain hammered the drum of the winch, the big spool at the bow that pulled divers up, with one good pull left in it if the storm didn't get there first. One-twenty. Still nothing out there to see, only the black and the rain coming through the black. Then the smudge stopped moving, forty meters out, big as a house, and no light anywhere on it.

The voice came across the water before the hull did, close, unhurried, pitched to carry over an engine. A man used to being heard.

"*Marrow.* Heave to. I'm coming along your port side, so don't waste a flare."

Sol set the mug down on the winch housing very carefully, the way you set a thing down when you want your hands free.

"Port side," Dey said. "That's the blind side."

"I know which side it is."

"He was already there," Wren said, and turned the slate around so they could all see the stopped smudge sitting on the screen with nothing to show for it but rain. "Ivo's been calling the backup channel four hundred meters west for two days and nobody's answered him. That's a tower Rusk swears is dead. If that voice is in there, it's the only thing down there still talking, and he's about to tell us so."
